title: Trick for trick, or, The debauch'd hypocrite a comedy, as it is acted at the Theatre-Royal by His Majestie's servants / written by Tho. Durfey.
author: D'Urfey, Thomas, 1653-1723.

plays.play_title: Trick for Trick: OR, The Debauch'd Hypocrite.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: A Pleurisie, I see it.

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: I rather hold it for Tremor Cordis.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: Dee' mark the Foeces? 'tis a most pestilent Contagious Fever—a Surfeit, a Plaguy Surfeit, he must bleed.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: By no means—

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: I say Bleed.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: I say 'tis dangerous, the person being so much spent beforehand, Hypocondriaque humours being now in full Power, and Nature drawn so low—No, I rather think Clysters, cool Clysters.

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: Now, with your favours—I shou'd think a Vomit; for, take away the Cause, the Effect will follow; his Stomach's foul, and the Intellect inflam'd.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: No, no, wee'l rectifie that part by milder means.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: Come Sir, you must have patience; Brother, I think we had best first clap on the Cataplasme.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Good Gentlemen, good Learned Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: And see those Broaths made ready within this hour; Come Sir, pray be rul'd.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Pray Sir will you leave me; I beseech you leave me: Convey your Cataplasmes to those that need 'em, your Vomits, and your Clysters.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: Bring in the Lettuce Caps—You must be shav'd Sir, and then wee'l make you sleep.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Ay, till Dooms-day—What unnecessary Nothings are these?

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: How do ye Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: What Questions they propound too—how do you Sir, I'm glad to see you well.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: Open your Mouth, I pray Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Aw—well, can you tell me now how old I am?—There's my hand, pray shew how many broken shins I shall have within these two year—'S'Death, who wou'd be thus in Fetters, good Mr. Doctor, and you Dear Doctor, and the third sweet Doctor, and precious Master Pothecary, I beseech ye to give me leave to live a little longer—You stand before me like my Mourners.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose:
A great Distemper, his fancy now begins to turn too.

Pish, what more hindrance still?—Sir—'tis not our Custome to be rude—but dismiss your Company with what haste you can; for we must minister within this half hour.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Oh,—a fair riddance, my learned Horse-leeches.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Be not uncivil, Tom,—and use your pleasure—I know she will be here to visit him within this half hour: Do what you can to win her, but use no violence.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I will not 'faith.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Where, where's this Sick Man?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Where are the Women, Man? there's my Province. Methinks these Women—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Thou think'st nothing else.—

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: See Franck—here's two of thy Friends come to visit thee; Prithee look up—and bid 'em welcome—I'll go and see if they have got any thing for thee to eat—Come, sit up, and be merry, Man.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How do'st thou, Franck, ha?
Come, give me thy hand, and bear up boldly—what, shrinck ith' Sinews for a little Sickness? a petty, puny, paultry Fever—Pox upon't, sing it away, Man.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: I am on the mending hand, I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How like a Flute thou speak'st, on the mending hand? Gogs boars I'm well—Speak like a Man of honour.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Thou art a Mad Fellow; what, never staid. Tom?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Let Rogues be stai'd that have no habitation, a Gentleman may wander—turn thee round, Franck—and see what I have brought thee—Sirrah, open the Scene and let the Work appear—Francis, a Friend at need is worth a Million.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: What hast thou there, a Julip?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: He must not touch it, 'tis present Death.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ye are an Ass—
Thou minister? thou mend a Pack-Saddle-You must pardon him—my Friend Franck—but a plaguy simple Fellow.
Do'st thou see this Bottle?—Prithee view it well; Agen observe it.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Well, I do, Tom.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: There are as many Lives in't as a Cat carries; It refines the Spirit, revives the Person, removes the Disease, Restores the blood; heats, nourishes, fills the Veins, Cures, comforts, warms, purges—hey—in fine, 'tis everlasting Liquor—and shou'd be spoken of with reverence.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Prithee what is't?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Why 'faith—Old Sack.
Old Spirit stirring Oyly, reverend Sack—which, maugre any thing I can read yet, was the Philosopher's Stone The Wife King Ptolomy did all his Wonders by.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Nay, I see no harm Sir—if drunk with moderation.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Moderation!—Drink with Walnuts, Man, which I have ready here, and a Glass too; take me without my tools, and hang me.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Pray, Sir, use temperance, You know your own state best.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Temperance!—ugh, ugh—Pox on him, I had like to bin choak't with a Wall-nut-shell—by giving ear to his damn'd temperance.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: I thank thee, Iack—I shall be careful—Yet a Glass or two can do no harm, your Friend Tom is grown very sober.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
A fool, a fool, he minds nothing now

but Jelly-broth a mornings, and Bulking Whores at Night—Never cares for good Company, Fiddles, nor Glasses now—a very Coxcomb, that's the truth on't.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Where the Devil are these Women all this while?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: No, no, take my Counsel, Franck,
prose: Hang up your Julips, and your Portugal Possets, Your Barly Broths—and Sorrel Sops; I hate 'em—they are mangy and breed the scratches onely—I wonder she does not come all this while—Come Franck, here's to thee.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: With all my heart—and methinks I feel a strange alteration on the sudden—my pulse beats quick, and lively.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: So long, and yet no bolting.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, I knew 'twou'd come to that— my presence is a Never-failing Cordial to both Sexes; here, take this off thrice, and then cry Heigh, like a Huntsman, with a clear heart, and no more fits I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: Are the things ready? and is the Barber come?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: An hour ago, Sir?

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: Bring out the Oyles, then.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: S'death—here agen!—Now, or never, Tom, do me a kindness, and deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Deliver thee,—from whom?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: From these things that talk there, Physitians, Tom, Scouring-sticks, they mean to read upon me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I'll do't,—Come hither, Iack.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phys.
prose: We desire all to depart the Room, and no longer disturb the Patient.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Strike in with me for your part, and let us play upon these Rogues a little—for Look ye Doctor, suppose the Devil were sick now—his horns saw'd off, and his head bound with a Biggen—sick of a Calenture taken by a Surfeit of stincking Soules at his Nephews, and St. Dunstans, what wou'd you minister upon the sudden? Your Judgment short, and sound.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: A Fool's head.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No, Sir,—it must be a Physitian, for three causes; the first, because it is a ball'd head likely—which will down easily without Apple pap.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: A main cause.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: So 'tis, and well consider'd,
The second Cause, 'tis fill'd with broken Greek, Sir,
Which will so tumble in his stomach, Doctor, and Jumble and work upon the Crudities, the Faeces, and the Fiddle-strings, conceive me Doctor, that of meer reason they must dis-imbogue.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Or meeting with the Stygian humour.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Right, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Forc'd with a Cataplasme of Crackers.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ever.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Scour all before him, like a Scavenger.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Satis fecisti Domine—my last Cause.
My last, and not my least, most Learned Doctors,

Because in most Physitians heads—I mean those that are most excellent—and Old withal—and angry; I say, because in most Doctors heads, there is a kind of Toadstone Bread and Crust, Sir, — whose virtue—the Doctor being stript and laid upon a Grid-iron

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: What's that, Sir!—a Grid-iron?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Grid-iron, Sir! the Learned hold it necessary, then by an Instrument of his own Barber, his Nose being slit, incis'd, his Mouth gagg'd open, and his most bawdy excremental Tongue—bray'd in a Mortar—to Powder—the Cure's infallible, Not to be question'd.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: Bless me! what stuff's here? Mad Sir! what mean you?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Onely a Question—Nothing else—for say the belly ake caus'd by an Inundation of Pease Porridge.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: This is not civil.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I think not—that's all one: Or grant the Diaphragma by a Rupture—

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: The Sign being then in the head of Capricorne.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Meet with the Passion Hypocondriaca, and so cause a Carnosity in the Kidneys, must not the Brains being butter'd with this humour cause a Cathartique Motion? answer me that.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: What shall we answer ye? what shall I say? Ye are an Ass, will that satisfie ye?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Out still—for the Ass is yours by your long Ears, your Nose too which I will pull thus into form, and take possession of a Sattin Cap to give your thick Skull, and your Brains more aire.

speeches.speaker: 2. Phys.
prose: Come, come, let's be gone Sirs, we are abus'd.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No 'faith, not yet, but shall be in good time—then if my Ladies Dog be laxative, troubled with qualms, grumblings, Windy Cholicks, Doctor; are ye therefore to open the Port Vein, or the Port Esquiline? your answer quickly.

speeches.speaker: 3. Phys.
prose: I'll answer no more—farewel, Sir, the next Fit you have, Bedlam shall find a Salve for; we came to do you good, But these young Roarers it seems have bor'd our Noses.

speeches.speaker: 1. Phys.
prose: Drink hard, and get unwholsome Wenches, 'tis ten to one then we shall hear further from your note alter'd.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: And wilt thou be gone, sayes one?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: And wilt thou be gone, sayes t'other?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Then take the odd Crown, to mend thy old Gown, And wee'l be all gone together.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Ha, ha, ha,—most excellent Rogue, I love thee heartily for this.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Sir, the Young Ladie—sent me to see what Company ye had with ye—and whether they may make a Visit?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Pray tell 'em, with all my heart—they'l much honour me in't—You see my Company.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come hither Crab—is not my Mistress one of 'em?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: And who else?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose:
Madam Sabina
.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Oh—heark Sirrah, not a word of my being here; Take that, and Mum.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: You have ty'd my Tongue up, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Ah—nay if you look so brisk, farewel the Fever, Friend.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Nay, I am much better, thank my Dear Tom here.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: The Game is ready to begin, your Mistress is coming.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I know it, therefore sit still good Franck, and not a word of me till you hear from me—then as you find my humour, follow it. You two come with me, and let us stand close, unseen—I warrant thee I catch her.

speeches.speaker: Sab.
prose: How dee' Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: The favour of this Visit from you, Madam, gives me strength to tell ye, That my Enemy has done his worst; I am growing well agen.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: I am glad to hear it—Were you ever sick before, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Of Love, Madam, not else.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Of Love? Alas! for ye—but you had good hopes of your side. You know 'twas no Epidemick distemper; for 'tis as impossible, a man shou'd dye by Love, as that he shou'd live by it—and either of these are Miracles this Climate never produces.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No, no—I have no hope, nor is it fit Friend—my life has been so lewd, my loose condition, which I repent too late, so abominable, That nothing but despair stands now before me.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Who's that, Sir—another Sick Man?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: In all my Courses shameless—disobedience.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Sure, I shou'd know his voice—Pray, Sir, who is't?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: One that you little thought to have seen in such a condition; 'Tis the Wild Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Who my Monsieur?—Monsieur Thomas? ha, ha, ha, this is some trick.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: You'l think better, when you see him—he was seiz'd yesterday with a strange distraction—a perfect madness.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: That's like enough—he has been seiz'd with that, ever since I knew him.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Not in this Nature, Madam; he is now, since he came to himself, much afflicted in's mind—he came hither to ask pardon of me for some things done long since, which his distemper made to appear like wrongs; but 'twas not so.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Sure that is not possible.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Here he comes—Pray observe him.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Come, Sir, be comforted.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: To what end, Gentlemen—when all is perish't upon a wrack. Is there a hope remaining, the Sea, that never knew sorrow shou'd be pitiful—my Comfort's gone, my Life has made me Wretched—Nor is it possible, were I to live Ten Ages, Ever to recall the least part of my Follies.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Oh you despair too much. Madam, you see his condition, One word from you may yet recover him.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: I know not what to do, nor what to think—I am amaz'd 'twixt pity and admiration.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: If it be real, 'tis no Jesting matter; a Man is not so soon made, Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: What are these Ladyes?—I had a Sister once, a Virtuous Sister, But I abus'd her—poor Soul, I wrong'd her—a Mistress too, a Kind sweet Beauteous Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Now, Madam, now's your time; now he's talking of ye.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: I'll do any thing, rather than see him thus.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I wrong'd her too—I sent her a damn'd Letter full of Oaths, Wrack't her poor Innocent Ears with Damms and Devils, Wo worth the time I did so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Now, Madam, speak, or never.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: By Heaven, I will; ah little do you know how my heart bleeds for him.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—she comes apace—the Rogue counterfeits rarely.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Oh my fortune. But 'tis but Just I be despis'd and hated.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Despair not, 'tis not Manly—Now Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: How dee' Sir? pray be comforted—give me your hand—you us'd to meet this kindness with more haste; I swear I pity ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: By Heaven 'tis she—oh goodness! not to be equall'd—let me thus low implore thy pardon; I have been wild and wicked, I confess it, but ah dear Saint, consider on our frailties; Youth often wanders from the way, and—

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Indeed Sir, you shan' not kneel.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Not kneel? oh name it not, my Crimes are many, and nothing but repentance, low repentance—Iack.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I, I mind ye—proceed and she's thy own, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Nay then I'll kneel too—for I have faults too many, I shou'd beg your pardon too, all things consider'd.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Precious—Dearest, Lovely—Charming—Ah,

all my whole lifes service—cannot merit half, half this blessing.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Where, where's my Master?—oh Sir—the Fidler, Sir, is not at leisure yet, but he will be about half an hour hence. But I have got Sir, according to your order, a couple of the finest Black fat Whores yonder—'gad the Jades do so tumble about—ha, ha—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Damn'd Dogg—

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: 'S'death—this damn'd dull Rogue will spoil all—what, what's that you say, Sirrah? who wou'd you speak with, ha?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, an Impudent Dog, who wou'd he speak with?—here's no body here knowes him—Kick him out o' doors there.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: What, not know Launce?—I am Launce, Sir, and a Pox take me, if I have not two of as fine fat Whores as a man wou'd desire to lay his Leg over.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Oh Heaven! I'm betray'd! and this was onely a design upon me. I find it now 'tis so, Cousin—oh I cou'd curse my self now for being so credulous—this was a Plot betwixt 'em, and now by chance discover'd; stand off, and touch me not, Base Fellow—Come, let's away—Farewel Sir, and when you are mad next—let your fat Whores administer.

speeches.speaker: Sab.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—this was a pleasant Jest.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come ye hither, Sirrah, and lay your head down on this Chair, I'll be merciful to ye—I'll onely cut your Ears and Nose off; Your head shall scape—doo't quickly, Rogue, or I will hew thee into Mammocks.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Oh for Heavens sake, Sir, what mean ye? You know I did nothing but what you bid me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ah—Insipid Whelp.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Hang him, let him wear his Nose a little longer—'Twill spoyl the fashion of his face else.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Though 'twas unluckily, 'twas Ignorantly done, and let him live to make amends.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Pox on't—when I had bent her like a twigg—brought her to my hand—made her quite sure, my own, with art and Industry, and to be bubbled of her in the very last moment, by the negligence of a Dog, a Hound, a Son of a Whore, a plague—Prithee Val, let me have but one pass through his Guts, and I'll forgive him.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Oh Gentlemen, for heavens sake hold him—for my guts are so empty, that he may easily rip 'em open.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Come forgive him—the Rogue I dare swear did it out of meer Kindness.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: By my Eight Languages, and so I did—I was so overjoy'd to bring him the good News, that I never minded who was with him.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Devil on't—this is alwayes my damn'd fortune, and I have still observ'd if a Fool be in a Family—where any Person has a design—if his Ignorance does not discover it, his ill fortune will—and that's as bad—Well, I am resolv'd she shan'not scape thus—I will have one more bout with her. You will not leave me, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not I 'faith; I will not miss the sport.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Nor I—but when shall it be?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: To Night at her Window in a Serenade.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: With all our hearts—Franck, wou'd thou wer't well to go too.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: I know not, 'tis as I feel my self—but it may be I may venture, For I can walk I find.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Go Dog, get you to my Father, and tell him my last Nights Ramble, I'll come and second ye; away—I shall get the Rogue this way a beating at the second hand.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Yes, Sir. I am glad I'm got off so well; for I was damnably afraid of losing my Ears, and Nose. Well Sir, I'll go and carry the Whores to the same Bulk, where I found 'em, and then let 'em seek their fortune.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Sirrah, that shall be my task.
Come Friends, let's prepare for the business; till Night I am employ'd—but then I am for ye.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Now to the business of Matrimony—I think I have got one here will fit me—I pickt her up in the Piazza's, what she is I know not, nor do I care—so she be fruitful and sound—Set down the Candle, Sirrah, and get you gone—Come hither Mistress—Let me see your Face—those Eye-browes are your own, I hope?

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Yes, I assure you, Sir— I counterfeit nothing.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Very well—now walk before me—let me see you pace a little. ah—trip—trip—thus, thus—I wou'd have my Woman do so.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Sir, I shall quickly learn to please ye, there shall be nothing wanting in my duty, to act, or to observe.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Prettily said—as to your age, Madam, I guess you to be about Five and twenty—something over—a good ripe age, I like that well enough—Pray open your Mouth; I think you have all your teeth.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: I hope so, Sir—they have had easie service.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: And wilt thou sing?

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Pleasantly, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: And drink?

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Profoundly.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: And swear—and tell a Story after Supper?

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: As you think fit, Sir — by the way of rellish, or so.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Give me thy hand then, she's honest, I know by that; for she that simpers, and talks of Religion alwayes, proves to be the greatest Jilt—who waits there?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Your pleasure, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose:
Bid my Daughter come hither—now I think I shall be even with my Monsieur— my sneaking Ananias: For I will get upon her Body. Demi-Gyant that shall play the Hector at his Nurses Breast, and beat a Constable in his swadling Cloathes.

Come hither Mistress—pray respect the Lady whom I intend to make my Wife, your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: How Sir!

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Now you shall find me so then—what a pox, d'ee think I'll leave my Inheritance to Pins, and Bodkins, to Towers, Jesamine Gloves, and Trimmings—to a leaky Vessel—that cannot keep my name up when I dye to thee?

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: You have a Son, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Who?—where is he? who is he like?

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: Your self.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Thou ly'st—thou hast spoyl'd him, Thou, and thy Prayer-Books;—he my Son? No, I disclaim him, And all that speaks of him. Why, did not I catch him singing yesterday a godly Ballad, to a godly tune too, and in one of his Pockets a Catachisme with the Creed in great Letters at the beginning?—No, Damsel of the dark—I know he's one of your Disciples, he wou'd be rul'd else.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: Mine?—'tis a sign then you know little of his humour, That can believe I have power to turn him any way.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Huswife I know it, and expect to be rewarded, what Tavern has he us'd since he came over? what things done, that showes a Man and Mettle? when was my house at such a shame before, to creep to bed at ten and twelve for want of Company? No singing, nor no dancing, nor no drinking?—thou think'st not of these scandals—thou can'st snore, and sleep, and Chatter bawdy in thy Dreams,—and the next morning wake and go to breakfast, and nothing else—but his life shou'd be otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: So it is, Sir—believe me, for I speak it to my knowledge, he's as mad as heart can wish; as debauch't a Fellow as any in the Suburbs.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Women, Sir, will talk, but you know we must bear with that sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Well, now I think on't, I will try the Boy once more, it may be he does but counterfeit, and then I'm happy—go, get you in, I'll keep you close enough, lest you break loose, and do more mischief to him—Within there.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Dee' call, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Go presently, and seek the Boy, and bid him wait my pleasure in the morning—d'ee hear, Mark what house he's in, and what he does—and tell me truth.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: I will not fail, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
verse: Youth may delight to boast of Act or Skill,
But the pleasure of an Old Man—is his Will.
prose:
If ye do, I'll hang ye. Come, Madam—I must desire you to stay here, till he comes, and

then wee'l settle all—there's your apartment, there you'l find all necessaries—Now if he prove but right, he has all yet; If not, this other way shall make an end on't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: AT Valentine's house so merry?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: As a Lark, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: So frollicksome, do'st say?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: I'm sure I heard it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ballads, and Fiddles too?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: No, but one Fiddle, but twenty noises.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Did he do Tricks?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Ah, the rarest Tricks, Sir—here's my Fellow Launce, he can Inform ye all, he was among 'em, and as mad as any there; I stood up in a Corner.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Come, Sir—what can you say?—Is there any hope yet your Master may return?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Put your hand into your Purse—and give me an Angel, Then perhaps I may tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: How, how? an Angel?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: An Angel, Sir—'Faith not a Farthing under, such things, such roaring things—an Angel, Sir, quickly, come.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: There 'tis, damn'd Rogue, thou hast found my blind side.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ay, ay, Sir, that's all one—so—well now Sir, by the Virtue of 8: Languages, by the Faith of a Traveller and a Gentleman, Your Son is found agen, the Son—the Tom.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Is he the Old Tom?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: The Old Tom.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Proceed then.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Next to consider how he is the Old Tom.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ay, handle me that.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: I wou'd you had seen it handled last night, as we handled it—Cap-a-pe, i'faith—oh the noise, the noise we made!

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Good, good, i'faith, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: The house beset around—the Windowes Clatt'ring, and all the Chamber-Maids in such a hurrey, one with her Smock half off, Another in haste with a Hose upon her head.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: A Fellow railing there out of a Loupe-hole, and his Mouth stopt with dirt.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, hah, ye Rogue.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Another peeping out with his greasie Night-Cap on, and a Torch popt in's face to clear his eye-sight.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—Dog.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: The Gentleman himself, young Monsieur Thomas, environ'd with his furious Mermydons, the fiery Fidler and my self, Now singing, now beating at the Doore, there parlying—Courting at the Window, at the other, scaling.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: And all these several Noises to two Trenchers strung with a Clew of Brown Thred—which show'd rarely.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha,—rarely well—rarely well.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Well, well—what d'ee mean, Sir—Your blowes are not well I'm sure, nor will my shoulders long, if you hold on at this rate.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: I'faith I beg thy pardon—I was so transported, I did not know what I did—there's money for thee to make thee amends—eat, and grow fat agen.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Nor here, Sir, gave we the Frollick over.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: What, more yet? why this is admirable.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: More, ay, and the best too, Sir—for at last we quit the Ladies house on composition—and to the silent Street turn'd all our furies. A sleeping Watchman here we stole the shooes from; there make a noise, at which he wakes and followes—then cryes out Theeves, and throwes his Bilboe at us— and Wades the Kennel in no footed stockings.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Oons—this is the rarest Boy, ha, ha—

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Windowes and Signs we sent to Erebus—a cry of Butchers Currs we entertain'd last, and having let the Pigs loose in out-Parishes, made every Street look like a Bear-Garden.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Instead of Bears, and Bulls, a Rogue, a Rogue.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Down—comes a Constable—and the Sow his Sister, most villainously tramples upon authority—there a whole Stand of Rug Gowns routed Manly, and the King's Peace put to flight—the Constable rallyes again—when, Sir, a Purblind Pigg—runs me his dirty Snout into his Lanthorn—out goes the light, and all turns to confusion.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: But, Sir, the best Jest was, a foolish Potter needs wou'd know the matter—opens his door, when, mark the Fate of Cuckolds, a Boare imbost takes sanctuary in his Shop, and Twenty Dogs rush after—We still cheering, down goes the Pots, and Pipkins—down the Pudding-Paus—the Cream-Bowles cry revenge here; There the Candlesticks; oh such a noise.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
verse: Ha, ha, ha,—
If this be true, thou little Tyny Page,
This tale thou tell'st to me,
Then on thy Back will i presently hang.
A handsome new Livery.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: How now, where's my Son?

speeches.speaker: Servant,
prose: He's here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Now Sir—you shall hear all—and laugh abundantly, he has such a grace in telling it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Son Thomas—I am glad to see ye, and to hear of ye; You may be now my Son agen, if you please, and enjoy the blessings attending it—but come, because I feel a scruple in my Conscience, concerning your late carriage—and therefore like Father wou'd be satisfied; To clear all, Thomas, get you upon this Table.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: This Table, Sir? Lord, how you are misled!—what strange fancies are these? fitter for Fools and Mad-men.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: What, what?—come, come, I say, get you on this Table. and Instantly, I'll have it so.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Well, Sir, you must be obey'd.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: So—now Thomas, like a most compleat Gentleman come from Tripoly—relate your last Night's Frollicks, mince at nothing—but let me have it freely as 'twas acted—'twill please me best.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Verily, Sir—though Age and Youth, and Youth and Age are different, different I mean divided 'twixt themselvs in point of reason; Nay, though our eyes are blinded, that is, though we cannot see.

I say—yet I say agen—or 'tis no matter whether I say it agen or no, That Reason, and Religion, shou'd Instruct Age to better courses than Blindness guides them to. Reason, and Religion are two worthy persons, and shou'd Instruct a wandring Mortal—Ah, Sir, remember—remember, I say, Take notice, place it in your Bosome—in your Heart, in your—I say, remember—that is, do not forget—but remember.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Hey day, he's preaching—you Rogue Launce, You lying Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Gad forgive me, will ye spoyl all agen, Sir?—What a Devil d'ee mean?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Away, Sirrah, and summon the rest of the Family hither, that I may edifie them all. Sir, you keep a Company of sawcy Fellowes, debauch'd, and daily Drunkards, that devour ye. Things, whose Souls tend to the Cellar onely.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Sirrah, give me my Money agen, or—

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Why Sir, let me never eat agen—or feel the Blessing of another new Livery, if he be not the very Devil in Debauchery, Sir: And what I have told you of him is all true; ask Robin here.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Nay Sir, the truth is, I did see my Young Master pick up two Whores, and put 'em into Pudding-Lane.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'Tis strange these Rascals—but Sir, when Folly and Idleness take the upper hand of Reason, and permit when they meet and Inhabit the Heart, the Mind, the Soul, the Faculties, the—'Tis a hard matter—'tis, I say, a—matter of difficulty, of difficulty—a matter of moment—and all that, Sir, to reform or conform, or direct, or dispute, or disswade—or divine, or dispose, or—

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Or the Devil and all; come down, I say. Bless me! what stuffs here?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Sir, are ye mad? stark mad? did not I see ye beat a Constable last Night?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I touch authority, ye Rascal? I violate the Law?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: No, no, he had rather preach to him—Lancelot du Lake, Get ye upon adventures—cast your Coat, and make your Exit.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Pur l'amour de Dieu.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Pur me no purs—but get you out at that Doore there; Out ye Eight Languages.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: My blood upon your head Sir—Did not I tell you 'twou'd come to this? What shall I do to live now? if I beg, I shall be Whip't; and if I steal, I shall be hang'd. What shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Heark ye, Sirrah; I'll provide for ye—go instantly and get the Fidler I order'd ye—let him be sure to be ready—and then go and

tell Vall and Iack I'll meet 'em within this half hour in the Rounds.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Now, now, Sir, dee hear him now?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Sirrah, a word, and I'll cut your Throat—away.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Out of my doors, Sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, ay, purge 'em all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: I shall Sir—and you too presently. Go Sirrah, bid my Maids that stand without—come in—I will have one shall please me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'Tis most fit Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Bring in the Money there—here Mr. Thomas.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: What you please Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: This money I give you, because heretofore you have been thought my Son—and by my self too—and some things done like me; Ye are now another—here is two hundred pounds, a civil summe Sir, for a young Civil Man: Much Land and Money wou'd (I suppose) now onely prove temptations, to take you from your settled and sweet carriage.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How's this? but Sir, I hope—

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Nay, I beseech ye, cover Sir; ye owe me no respect—I have nothing to do with ye; nor have you with my Estate Sir; Nor with this money neither, now I think on't—you can preach well Sir—Pray get a Tub—and deal about your Hums and Ha's with reverence; some of the Rabble perhaps may have farthings.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'S'death, I shall be finely bubbled if this hold—lose all my Fortune for a Frollick—I must wheel about agen, there's no remedy.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: I have one thing more to say before we part Sir. Behold those females there, pray view 'em well: I want a right Heir to Inherit me, not my Estate alone, but my conditions, from which you are revolted—therefore dead—And I will break my back, but I will get one.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Will you chuse there, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose:
There, among those Damsels—in my own Tribe, I know their qualities—which cannot fail to please me, for their Beauties—a matter of three farthings makes all perfect. A little Beer, and Beef-broth—they are sound too—stand all abreast—Now Mr. Thomas, before I choose—You having liv'd long with me, and happily, sometimes with some of these too, which fault I never frown'd on—Pray

shew me (for fear we confound our Genealogies) which you have laid abroad: Speak your mind freely, Have you had Copulation with that Damsel?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I have.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Say ye so? Pray how?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How, is not seemly here to say, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Stand you aside then—What say you to'th' second, Thomas?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: With her too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: With her too? ha, ha—the Rogue wins upon me strangely.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: So, so, he's coming agen.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Retire you two—speak forward Mr. Thomas.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I will, and to the purpose—even with all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: How? with all? that's somewhat large, with all Thomas?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: All, surely Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose:
A sign thou art my own yet—in agen all, and to your several Functions—Mrs. I pray come hither—

Tom, here's a Lady—that I found my self,

What think ye of her? she I'm sure's a stranger to ye.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: Mercy upon me, He here! nay then, I shall be murder'd.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: What, what's that? do'st know her Tom?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Know her? Why Sir, every Bulk about Town knowes her; I met her drunk i'th' Strand t'other Night, with twenty Boyes about her—I have thrown her into the Fleet Ditch—three several times for my share.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Go, get you gone too—and to your Bulk agen, my Marriage fit is over.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
prose: And thank ye too, rather than stay where He is.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Well, but what say ye to Luce, the Merchant's Daughter? she was too young—I think, when you travell'd some twelve years old.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Her will was Fifteen, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—'Faith well answer'd to cut off long discourse, Thomas, for I have many yet to ask ye of, Where I may chuse, and nobly—hold up one finger;—where I may not, two—or more; What think ye of Valeria? whose husband lyes a dying now—why two and in that form.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Her husband is recovered, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: A Witty Moral—have at ye once more, Thomas—the Sisters of St. Albans—what all five?—ha, ha, that Boy, that's my own Boy—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Still hoping for your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Pshaw, there needs none—a pox on pardon—I am pleas'd with thy confession, Nor will I think of Marriage any longer; for o'my Conscience I shall be thy Cuckold—there, there's Twenty Guinneys for ye, Sir. Go, and be merry—I see some sparkles which may flame agen; and if they do, thou'rt mine yet—farewel Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: So—'tis better thus, than t'other way however—but now to my Serenade—I have such a kind of a Mungril Love for this Woman—that I must, and will enjoy her, come what will on't—Oh Sirrah—well, hast got him?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: I Sir, I have been here—a rare Rogue—hee'l Fiddle and make a noise, but the Devil a stop he knowes, or when he fiddles in Tune. Good Sir—do something now—some roaring thing, that we may live and eat agen—By my 8. Languages I have had but one poor mouldy Crust this two daies.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Pox on thee for an eating Rogue, Nothing but Famine frights thee—Come hither, Sirrah, what Ballads are you seen in best?—ha? let's hear.

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
prose: Under your Masterships Correction, I can sing the Merry Ballad of Diverus and Lazarus. The Rose of England. In Creete when Dedimus first began. Ionas his Crying out against Coventry—and a merry Song, how Blind Toby and his Dog fell in Love with a Fair Lady, by seeing her play upon a Cymbal.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Very well. What else?

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
prose: Maudlin the Merchant's Daughter. The Devil, and the Dainty Dames.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Rare still!

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
prose: The Landing of the Spaniards at Bow; With the Bloody Battel at Mile-End.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: All you that would your good Old Fathers Cheat,
And e're his Death, do Covet his Estate;
To all his humours strict Compliance give,
For Age that doates once, has not long to live.
prose:
Excellent! Well Sirrah, go, and put him to his Stand, and let my Friends be ready—I'll follow ye.

I have heard, that sometimes Importunity gets more than Love: And 'Faith, I'll haunt her like a Ghost, but I'll have her. ha, ha, ha—It makes me laugh too, to think how I have Bobb'd my Father—had I been wild at first, he wou'd have been weary by this time; but now all's sure and settled.

segments.head: ACT IV. | SCENE II. A Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Franck.
prose: Whatever your Nice humour, Madam, seems to declare now, I am sure you must needs sometimes be of a contrary temper—he is my Friend I acknowledge; and the least thing I can do in his absence, is to speak well of him.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Sir, that freedome is of necessity allow'd, and whatever his Merit is, your Generosity cou'd not do less—but my knowledg of him and his temper, is proof against all your assertions; I will allow him for a general Man, and good Company; but let me tell ye—such a one though he makes the best Servant—certainly makes the worst Husband in the World.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Ay, that is, Madam, according as you order him. If you give him liberty, 'tis true, Men are apt to follow the Dictates of their own humours—but when you have the Bridle in your hand, methinks 'tis easie stopping the course.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: That, Madam, does not so much depend on your own power, as on your husband's temper; for if he be rough and passionate, you have so much Judgment to know your bounds. But, if mild, and soft natur'd—Your Province is the larger. And there are two things which ruine such a man—Fondness and Folly; for a man that is too fond of his Wife, is as certain to be made a Cuckold by her—as that she wou'd if she cou'd do't—were he never so ugly, or Jealous.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: If good Phrases, and Reason might pass for Jests, I swear you are the merriest man I know.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: I shou'd be glad, Madam, I cou'd breed your Diversion any way; though to the rest of the World, 'tis my ambition they shou'd rellish me more in the Philosopher, than the Buffoon.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Fye, fye, a better word than that, Sir,—Call a Witty brisk Fellow, that breaks a Jest onely for the sake of good Company, or so, a Buffoon?—Fye, I swear 'twas ill said.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Ay, 'tis a sign he has been sick lately.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: I do but think how you'd look, if Monsieur Thomas shou'd hear of this—you had best call Him Buffoon too.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose:
No, He's the General of 'em,—and the onely Person that I know can be allow'd of in that nature; for he has Wit in his Buffoonry—and a graceful action, gives an excellence to his Jest.—If he tells a Lye,

he will be sure it shall be a pleasant one: And he never tells a bawdy story for its own sake, but the Companies, and the Mirth that followes after.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: What think ye of this, Cousin?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Pish—Prithee what shou'd I think of it?—heark! what noise is this?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: But I have seen some dull Rogues Mangle a good Story so barbarously—how now? what's that?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Was ever the like known?—there is such a rout at your Window yonder—such shouting, such singing, and such a dismal noise—

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Noise? what noise? who is it?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: The mad Gentleman that us'd to ask for Madam Cellide, and twenty more, fidling, singing like Mad-men.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: 'Tis he—shall I never be at rest? who can endure this?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: He's as good as his word I see.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Heark ye, Cousin—now if you love me, let's put a trick upon him—I have a rare device in my head.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: I know this is against the grain, but come, I'll second ye.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: 'Tis a mad Rogue—but I know she loves him; I'll go up to my Closet-Window and see the sport.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Stand close now, and every one mind his business, Iack keep you that door there—and be sure none of her Servants enter, or go out—if any Woman pass, she is lawful Prize—Cut off all Convoyes.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis not fit I am seen—I'll therefore stand at distance and observe ye.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Ay, but heark ye Tom—who shall answer this?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Why, I shall answer it, Sir;—You fearful Puppy I shall appear to th' Action.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Well, well, I have done—we may talk too, may we not?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: With any Woman freely.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: And sing too, ha?—for there's my Master-piece.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No, Sir, by no means. I am the Man reserv'd for Aire—'tis my talent, and the Devil's in't if my voice don't charm her; heark ye, You may Record a little—Whistle, or so—to shew you are good at something—but for main singing—let me alone; away, be careful.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: But there's another thing; we may be beaten.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'Faith, so thou may'st—and well too—for thou deserv'st it richly—Why, what Bug-bears are in thy Brains? Beaten?—why who shou'd beat thee?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Why she may have men enough.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, art not thou man enough too?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I warrant thee—there's a low Window—I'll peep in and see what they are doing.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come Sirrah, let's hear some of your Art now—Nay, nay, No tuneing as ye love me—let thy Fiddle speak Welch, or any thing that's out of all tune—the Viler, still the better—like thy self—for I presume thy voice will make no Trees dance.

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
prose: Nay, truly you shall have it even as homely.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: With all my heart, keep it to that Key still—I think they are all abed.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: I think so too, Sir—I can hear no stirring any where, No light in any Window, 'tis a Night for the purpose, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come, strike up a flourish—and Sirrah, do you sing the Serenading Song I taught ye t'other Night; Wee'l bear the Chorus.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose: Who's there? what noise is this?—what Rogue at these hours—dares disturb us thus?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Oh what is that to you ye Fool?
Oh what is that to you?
Pluck in your face—ye bawling Ass,
Or I will break your Nose.
With a hey downe, downe, downe, downa.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose:
Tom—here's rare sport—here's one of the Women washing her Legs—Ah Rogue!—'Faith she has a fine plump Calf—ha, ha,—now she is come to her Knee—

oh—murder, murder—I'm kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Hah!—his face all bloody?

Hold still Iack, let me see, Where's the Wound? this is no jesting matter.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I know not, I feel none—cannot you see it?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ha, ha—I find it now—this was only a trick, a squirt of blood and a Pistol fir'd off—are they so frollicksome? have at 'em once more.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: 'Troth I'm glad I'm alive for all that—I'll go and get my face wash't, and come agen.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come Sirrah, now sing the English Ballad.

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
verse: There was a Noble Merchant
That lived in a Town,
He had an onely Daughter,
That was both fair and brown;
Sing hey trangdillo, dillo down.
A Noble Knight likewise,
On whom Fortune did frown,
He got her Maidenhead once in thrice,
Sing hey trangdillo down, down, derry down.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No stirring yet?—I believe the Devil has charm'd 'em asleep. Come, flourish agen, and the t'other Song—

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
verse: The Twelfth of April on May-Day,
My House, and Goods were stolne away.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Hold, hold—she comes—Sirrah, give me the Address I gave you in writing t'other day.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: O Lord, Sir, the Mice eat it in my Pocket one Night, but I have the Complement here that you took out of the Book of Common Places.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: That then, Sirrah, quickly—holdup the light—Madam. Were there no other light but your eyes—the World wou'd need no Sun—And—Conf—conserve me, Madam, if, like a Fly, I can forbear buzzing about that light—though I have burnt my Wings—ha? what think ye of that, Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Who wou'd forbear loving a Man that has such several wayes of Gallantry?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
verse: Hush—you shall hear a Dialogue between us.
My Man Thomas did me promise
He wou'd Visit me this Night.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: What? Musical?—nay, let me alone for answering that.
I am here Love, tell me dear Love,
How I may obtain thy sight.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
verse: Come up to the Window my Love,
Come up to the Window my Dear;
Here's a Ladder of Rope,
That will help to guide thee up,
And thou sha't be lodged here.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: And 'Faith, I'll be with thee strait, she's very kind o'th' sudden, ha Sirrah? — go, all be gone, there's money.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ay Sir, so she is; you'l have good sport anon, ha?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Now Cousin—the Scuttle quickly.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Sir Eglamore that Valiant Knight,
Hey down, down a down;
So bruised was with grievous frights,
Hey down, down, downa down.
For he had been Cuffing so long with the Dragon,
That nothing could quench his thirst but a whole flaggon,
With a hey down, down, downa, &c.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
How now? what a Devil—is this?

Sirrah, Launce?—what is the matter I'm Inchanted, I cannot stirr—bound hand and foot.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Nay, my Dear—why are you so slow? Prithee make haste.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A pox on ye—Launce—what a Devil is this?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Come down, Sir, come down—they have plai'd some trick or other with ye—ha, ha—I thought so.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Fye, fye, so slow Sir; is this like a Mercurian?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'Faith I'll be even w'you presently—'S'death, a Basket! What Witches are these? — but I'll storm once more, and 'tis not Baskets, nor Chamber-pots, shall hinder me now; Sirrah, now sing.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Lucilla.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: I'm ready, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
verse: The Duke, he was a Noble Man, as any in the Town,

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Phoo, phoo—what's this? oh!

speeches.speaker: Fidler.
prose: But climbing to promotion, he suddenly fell down.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Death! this was another Trick upon me, I find by the Queans Mirth.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: What hast thou done?—not thrown him down I hope.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Onely a little way, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: A little way?—Oh heaven I'm undone! she has broke his Neck.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ha! is she so pitiful?—I may have a Trick then to recover all yet—oh my leg, my leg—I am spoil'd for ever; both my Legs.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Heark, heark, d'ee not hear him?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Shatter'd in twenty pieces, I'm undone! oh barbarous Woman! howl Sirrah, howl.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Oh, his back too! his back!—the bone is out of Joynt.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: D'ee hear ye Devil? run to the Surgeon quickly, fly: Or see my face no more. O horrid mischance! I come, I come.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Take heed of Women, Friends, take heed of Women; They'l put ye out of Joint—they'l shake your Souls out. Oh, ha, my Legg! my Legg!

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Your head, your head too, Sir—for your Skull being crack't, Your Brains may happen to catch cold. Ha, ha, ha! The Light's taken away, I believe she's coming.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: And cry out still—Men believe falsely that think Age makes 'em decrepid—No, 'tis Women, 'tis Women, oh—

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: She comes—she comes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Sirrah, squeeze out a tear, or two—Now for a swouning fit—ah!—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Where, where are ye, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: He's gone—he's gone. Master—sweet Master, here's Launce that calls—oh!—what shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Oh I am miserable! Sir, Sir—Dear Sir—Oh cursed Accident! help! help to hold up his head!

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ah 'tis stiff, Madam—every part of him is stiff; rub him, rub him.

speeches.speaker: Cellid,
prose:
Here, hold this Bottle of Amber to his Nose—Sir, Dear Sir, Open your eyes, and see my sorrow for ye; 'tis I that speak Sir.

For Heavens sake open your Eyes—I am here.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay—and—I am here too—and well—thank my Activity; Your Bottle of Amber will be unnecessary, And if thou scap'st me now—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: What, catch't agen! oh this subtle Devil!

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: However, I am bound in Conscience to thank you for your kindness—and since 'tis onely Trick for Trick, Madam, we have the more reason to be friends—I must needs own my self oblig'd t'ee; for the Devil take me if I have been kiss'd so heartily this great while.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—'tis strange your Legs shou'd be cur'd already Sir; But, Madam—he is such a Wagg—ha, ha—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Well—I have no other way, but seeming to comply.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come 'faith be kind now—I have a convenient Lodging here hard by—and one reconciling here now, will be worth Ages.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Fye! What baseness is this?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, that's all one—If I leave my self to a doubt agen—May I be Jilted as I have been—Come Sirrah, and help—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Hold Sir—well, now I see you love me; and believe Sir, this Impatiency has taken me far more than all your Addresses: Violence, will now be unnecessary.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ah, no Tricks, Madam—to be plain with ye, if you will marry me—so—if not, I am resolv'd to enjoy ye before I part, and then marry who you please.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Nay, that shall not need, I swear, if you have a Priest ready—I have try'd thee long enough; and though y'are a little Wild—I know you can love truly—ah my Dear Sweet!

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Why Ay. this is like something now,—Sirrah, have I not wrought her rarely?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ay, ay, but to her, to her Sir, don't let her cool.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come my Dear, shall we go in here, or to my Lodging?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Your Lodging, no indeed—I'll have the confirmation made here, follow me; but hold, 'tis convenient the Candle be out, for if my Cousin sees me, she'll so laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: 'Faith, well consider'd; besides, light in such a case is a little unnecessary—Sirrah, turn the Lanthorne—so.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: And will you always love me?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: This kiss shall confirm it.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
What ye Clown—with your Hat on? and to your Mistress too? You cou'd do no more if I were your Wife.

So, I am once more Conqueress, Now let him catch me if he can.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Who the Devil wou'd ha' thought, you should expect Ceremony in the dark?—Where, where is it Sirrah?—Oh here, Come, now let's go—I'm impatient till—S'death what's that?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ha! She's gone Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How! gone!

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: I have only leisure now to bid you good night Sir, and wish your leg well cur'd—to morrow perhaps, you may hear more.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Pox fetch thee—that's but the preamble. Still thus bubbled?—Sirrah help me to curse her. May she fall in love with an old man that's bed-rid, Afterwards, consider of it, despair, and then poyson her self with her own Mercury.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: May she be proud to that degree to scorn all her Sex, Then get the small Pox, and look like a Witch, that all her Sex may scorn her.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Well sed; or may—.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: May she get a great Belly by imagination—and when she hopes to see the precious Off-spring—may it prove Fire and Brimstone.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Men raile at Whores for Luxury and cost,
But believe me, all you that Iudgment boast,
'Tis your damn'd honest Women Iilt ye most.
prose: Well sed agen—Gad thou hast a pretty gift at it—but come, now let's be gone—and plot how to plague her to morrow, for if I leave her thus, may I lose all my Fame and turn Civilian.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: NOble Sir Peregreene, this unexpected favour of honouring my house with your Company is so far above my hopes—that I want words to express my sentiments of it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose:
Sir, your complements put me in mind of the Debt of

gratitude I owe ye—for my Daughters kind Entertainment:—I fear I have too much trespass'd upon your patience.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Fye Sir Peregreene, I thought you had known me better than to Imagine so poorly of me—your Daughter I assure ye has been a grace to my Family.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Any one Sir that has the good fortune to be in her Company will rather think it a blessing, then a trouble, especially if he be of my opinion.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Sir I thank ye, and 'twas a business of Moment that brought me hither; for yesterday in the afternoon I had a Letter from Sir Wilding Frollick—proposing a Marriage between his Son and my Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What, with Monsieur Thomas?

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: The same—I am so vext I forgot to bring it with me, 'twou'd have made you laugh heartily—for in my life I never saw so extravagant a style;—now Cousin my business in Town is, to put a stop to this Match, for I hear he comes often to her, and against her Will too,—does he so Cousin?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sometimes Sir—by way of visit, or so—but not against her consent, that ever I heard of, and you know Sir, 'twou'd not be civil in me to deny her visitants.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Cousin, you say well—but we Fathers perhaps have better eyes to pry into these matters—then your Youngsters have; she's a good Girl Sir, and I think a Fathers Indulgence shou'd be carefully imploy'd in bestowing a good Girl upon a good Man.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Oh all the reason in the World Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Why very well—then to be plain, his fame is none of the cleerest—for in troth we hear in the Country, he is ten times more mad, and debauch'd since he came from Paris, then he was before—they say, he never says his Prayers.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not publiquely I think Sir—but he may be the better for that.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose:
Oh no—and between you and I, I don't relish him—not like him I mean, and my Judgment. and good liking have gone hand in hand these 50 years—and think I am not crazy now Sir; there is an Imposition laid upon us Fathers—by the Law of Nature—to be Elaborate, and Zealous in our care for our Children; and though I profess t'ee Cousin, I entertaine no ill sentiments as to matter of his estate, I do as to the matter of his manners; mark me, I say his manners, for, believe me, however corrupt affections—put a false gloss upon a Fathers charge, yet it is certainly requir'd of him to be very circumspect

in his consideration, when it tends to the disposal of his Children; —but come, pray let me see her.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sir, Im afraid she's hardly stirring yet—but she'll soon be ready—I'll wait on ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Cousin, your very Servant.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: This Knight is as much affected with his formal Oratory as a Judge at the Sessions House, and if his humour hold, I fear may lose. his Mistress in spight of all his Intrigues.

speeches.speaker: Iack.
prose: how do'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Hylas
prose: 'Faith, better to see thee so well agen Franck, but prithee hast thou seen Tom today?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: No—what mad Rogues you were last night to make such a noise.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Did'st thou hear us? we were very frollicksome, that's the truth on't—for my part I thought he was mad.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Ay, but here's one come to Town, that will spoil his mad frollicks (her Father, Iack) he came early this Morning—and with intent to stop all proceedings.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Her Father! S'death what luck's this—where is he?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Gone in with Val. to see her—come, go with me, I'll help thee to the sight of him.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: With all my heart, it may be I may do him a kindness by it—Pox on him, has he smelt the business out already?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Sirrah, stay you there and watch—

Her Father in Town say'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Yes Sir, he came this morning; and since your bounty Sir has made me your Creature—I cannot but inform you that he is much incens'd against you—and if he sees you—he may perhaps fly into more Passion.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I'll be gone then. Damn'd Rogue, that he did not give me warning!

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Sir, There's no going out there, if you do you'l meet him, You must have a little patience—come hither—here's a standing Press—that my Master uses to hang Cloathes in, Get in here and you are safe, I'm sure they will not stay long.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Pox, mew'd like a Cat in a Cupboard—what damn'd luck's this!

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Cousin, it has been longer my study—therefore I shou'd know more of Men and Manners than you—Mum, mum—I say to you once more she shall not have him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sir, I am sorry he has the ill fortune to be no better known to ye; but 'tis fit your Judgment shou'd have precedency, especially, as to this affair.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—there in that Press say'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Yes, Madam, and I warrant in an Ague by this time.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Hush, not a word on't—I'll plague him for his last nights work; Sir I hope you know my Obedience is so settled, to believe my Youth shall never make me throw my self away upon a Man—you dislike—and one that I confess is the General of all mischief—and the lewdest, and most debauch'd person in Town.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: So—she has hit me to a hair—

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Her mind is very suddenly alter'd, or else this must be Cunning.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Child, remember my Caution, my blessing shall follow; and observe this as a Maxime, (which though not in Epithetus, yet is in Aratine—or some such merry Book, which in troth I have forgot) That the Marriage Bed is never happy, except the Father eats part of the Posset—'tis somewhat familiar, but the sence is strong.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Very strong Sir, and in my Judgment extends to many things.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: It does so. Do ye know this Man we speak of Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Some small acquaintance, Sir—his Person, not his humour.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Your name good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Hylas—at your Service—Sir Robert Hylas Son of Essex.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Indeed? let me embrace ye—your Father was my Intimate and good Friend; are you Sir Robert Hylas Son, say ye? By my faith, I am glad to see you. Your Father was the best Man of Land we had in Essex, when I knew him.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I think he had enough to keep him warm Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: And you I think are his Heir—let me embrace ye once more—'faith, I shou'd think my Daughter better bestow'd, if—but I'll not begin.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Hum!—his Daughter—Sir I have 15 hundred or so; this wou'd be rare—and she's a delicate Girle—Well—sit fast Monsieur Thomas—I never refuse blessings, I.

speeches.speaker: Sir. Per.
prose: A man of no Principles; no, I will not have you think of him.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: I will not Sir—but as of a Mad-man.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: A Whirligigg.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: A Monster—that on my Conscience—has more Wenches—that take pay of him, than the Grand Signior has.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: That's a lye, for I never paid a Whore in my life.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: What think ye Sir?—I'm sure you cannot but be more my Friend than his—Pray speak.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: 'Faith she seems willing too—well, I begin to be damnably in Love—this must be the Twentieth, I find it.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
Will you be so unkind to be silent, Sir?—I'm sure this

galls him. Is he not the basest fellow in Town?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: In Town? nay in Christendome—I think he's the greatest Corrupter of Youth, and Debaucher of Women in the whole World.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Rare Rogue!

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: I marry him? what, a Fellow that makes it his business to be wicked?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: That never considers on his latter end, but Wenches on to perpetuity.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Ay, and that never is out of a course of Physick, but to gain time to get in agen.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Right, Madam—that never will be found—nor I think hardly ever was.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Very well, the Rascall's witty now he thinks me absent, But I shall make you smart for this my damn'd Friend, I shall.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Is this done like a Friend, Iack?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: No 'faith; but 'tis like a man in Love, and that hopes to bubble his Friend tho.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Be not too confident of your success—there will be some danger in't; for you know he dares fight.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Ay, but he is absent now—why when I see him Man, I'll forswear all agen.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: The Rogue has a tender Conscience however.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Mr. Hylas—introth I like your humour, and Company so well, That I desire to have you acquainted with my Daughter; she's a good Girle Sir—Pray be familiar with her.

speeches.speaker: Cellide,
prose: Prithee, look on this Gentleman—'faith he pleases me well.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Sir, I cannot doubt but in a little time his Merit, and Witty conversation—will give me the content you receive in him—Now he frets rarely.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Still more strange!—sure 'tis not possible she can be thus flexible.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Prithee go, and address—I believe she has a mind to thee.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Your humble Servant, Sir—'tis a happiness too great; 'S'death, this is the Civill'st Old Fellow—I ever met with—Madam, be pleas'd to enroll me among your Vassals.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: My Father's pleasure prefers ye Sir—you may command me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Very fine—Faith I have been debauch'd to fine purpose if this last;—but the worst is, that this dull Rogue shou'd bubble me—'S'death I shan'not have patience.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: The Devil take me Val. if I can help this, 'tis a Fortune thrown upon me—and you know if it were your own case—

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I'll not be concern'd in't Sir—if you'l venture a Beating, You may do what you please.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: Sir, here's a suspitious Fellow, has been prying up and down the house for above this hour; I believe h'has stole something.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Jernie, stole something!—I'll be Judg'd by all dis Company, who look most like a the Thief, you or I.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: O Rascal, are you here? examine him Sir, here's one Plot or other contriving.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Sir—this is his Rascal, his Procurer—one that he employes to set his Whores for him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Oh—is he so—I thought there was more in't than ordinary, Bring him before me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sirrah, bear up boldly, and fear nothing, I'll stand thy Friend.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Well, well—and what have you to say to me you Son of a—I say Sir—what have you to say to me?

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I say, you are his Pimp, Sir—and by the leave of this Company shall be whipp'd, and toss'd in a Blanket.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ah no!—a Jirk or so, if you please—but no Blanket, That is a little too ungentile—Jernie, when did you ever see a Frenchman toss'd in a Blanket?—Where the Devil is my Master gone now?

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Stand by, Let me examine him; Friend, it agrees not with the reserv'dness, and solidity of your Countenance, to be so far forgetful of your self, as to embroile, Or rather Incumber your Wit, about this Criminal Affair.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Your Servant, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Come, be genuine with me—here's a Protector's half Crown for thee—two shillings five pence sterling—and let it be a Key to unlock thy heart—Do'st thou come upon any Sinister Design?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Sir, upon my faith—I stood there only to watch, that was all.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: To watch us—oh—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Plac'd as a Spy Sir—come deal freely, and I'll entertain thee; What new Pranck is your Master about?

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Tell that, I've another Protector for thee.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Why then Sir, to say the truth, my Master is a plaguy—Debauch't Fellow—he never goes to Church—he sayes there's no good Company there; and my business here was to give him warning—if any came to disturb him when he was with this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: 'Tis plain now he wou'd have ravish't her—go fetch me a Cudgel, I'le make you an Example.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: O Lord, Sir, what d'ee mean?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: There's for your Commendations, Dogg.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: How!—in the Press?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Ay, 'tis evident—he came to rob the house.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Nothing but confidence can bring me off, therefore have at 'em—well, Gentlemen—have you look't your fill?—pray observe me once agen; 'tis I, I assure ye.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: How!—has he heard all then?—what will become of me?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: This is a little uncivil, by your favour, to hide your self in my house without my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Hold Cousin—let me speak—Sir—to lay the Law t'ee, wou'd perhaps be insignificant, you not understanding it; Reason too is lost upon ye, because you are a Mad-man—Yet, though these two fail—anger—has its full power; Nor shall my Daughter want a Champion—whil'st she has a Father—You conceive me Sir—Prepare your self.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Take him at his word—I'll be thy Second.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: What, in a Game at Tennis?—but now I think on't, thou art too dull for that too—for thy Wit and Courage have been much of a stamp ever since I knew thee. Hush, not a word more—I'll talk with you anon, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: I shall be swing'd—I see there's no remedy.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Now for my faculty, I'm resolv'd this Jilt shall not carry it off so—Sir, since I see you are a Man of Honour, and Jealous, and mindful of Injuries, and for some reason best known to my self, being now resolv'd that all shall out—know, 'twas by your Daughters contrivance—that I was shut up here.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: My Daughters?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Very well, he's fetching it off with a lye, but that shan't do; —heark'ee, Sir, what d'ee mean by that?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Nay, Madam—what did you mean by it. Sir, for me to say she is honest

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Is a lye?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Oh Heavens!

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Wou'd not be, I confess, so like a Gentleman, but that she is given to subtlety, and wantonness—give me leave to confirm it; For to be faithful with you, this was the day appointed for a certain business 'twixt she and I. You understand me, to which purpose I was shut up there—'faith I must needs say much against my own good humour and Inclinations.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Umph—I begin to discern it now, this was a Plot—Huswife—see my face no more.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Oh horrid Impudence! Pray hear me speak, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sir, this must not pass, upon this Lady without better grounds.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Sir, you shall have what ground you please, and Where. What Madam, I warrant you are amaz'd at this?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: I do confess I am.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Heark ye, Sir—d'ee hear that?—she confesses it—after this—sure there's nothing remains to prove the truth of my Story: Madam, I am heartily sorry, it shou'd be my ill fortune to relate this—but you must pardon me—I do it for the discharge of my Conscience, and so your most devoted—heark ye, shall I lye with ye to night?—Be kind—I'll recover all yet—I'll stay half an hour for your answer at the next Tavern; consider on't—Gentlemen your Servant—and You Sir—

A part of whose Nose I desire to be oblig'd with as a remedy against my Cold—my kind good natur'd civil. Son of a Whore—Your Servant, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: Pox on him—what a plaguy twitch he gave me.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: I hope he has forgot me, but I must follow him, and if he will be contented with a Limb—I'm happy.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: My rage has almost suffocated me—but I'll instantly go and cut off the Intail of my Estate, and leave her as despicable as she has left her honour.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: Sir, let reason mitigate your passion, this may be all false.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: May be, upon my life it is—Pray Sir, let me speak a word with ye in private.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Infamous Creature!

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
Was ever such an Impudent lye carried so prosperously? By Heaven I was so confounded, I had no power to speak a word: I must have this recover'd, and suddenly, I'm undone else.—

He told me when he went — he wou'd stay for my answer at the next Tavern—go you instantly, and tell him I have consider'd, and desire to speak with him privately in my Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Yes, Madam, and I'll warrant I'll bring him back.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
I have one Trick more in my head, that if it prospers, is certain to recover all yet; for the Love I had for him is so turn'd in a desire of Revenge—that I cannot rest till it be done.
How, his Sister? she must know nothing.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: What, alwayes in Contemplation? shall I never find thee otherwise?—Why, thou hast quite deserted thy merry humour; Prithee Cellide, what ayl'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Now I think on't, her Company may be advantagious to me, If made use of rightly—Come—thou shalt know all, and I must therefore confess the subject of my thoughts was thy mad Brother.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: What, are ye reconcil'd? I am glad of that.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: In a fair way to't—hee'l be here within this hour, to confirm the bargain—and if I cou'd, I wou'd have his Father be by, and overhear it.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: I'm sure hee'l come willingly, for he's very much pleas'd with the Match, tho' our Father be against it.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Do, and I'll Order my Woman to place him conveniently.

speeches.speaker: Doro.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, we shall have rare sport.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Rare sport indeed—as I will order it—for his Father, and Sister to be by—when I put the Trick upon, will be a rare venture—heark, I think he's coming, I'll to my Chamber, and prepare for him.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: What, Sir, d'ee think I tell ye a lye?—I hope you see more grace in my Physiognomy—than to believe that.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay gad, if Deformity be a grace in a Woman—thou I confess hast a considerable share on't.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Come, good Sir, spare your Expressions till ye come to my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Away then—Sirrah, for the last business I forgive ye. But if you fail in your charge agen.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose:
No Sir, Ill be doubly careful now—I understand my Trade.

What a Devil, I have not been a Pimp so long for nothing.

segments.head: ACT V. | SCENE II. A Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: You shall find me bountiful—but be sure to do as I bid ye, and be all ready when I give the Sign, then leave the rest to me.

speeches.speaker: Servants.
prose: Madam, we will not fail.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Away then, and watch your time.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Madam, he's come.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: So. Is he alone?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: No Madam, his Man is with him.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Then 'tis as I wou'd have it; for I am resolv'd that Rascall shall partake in my revenge—be sure you are ready with a Rope when I give the word.

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Yes, Madam, I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: But first, go to my Father, and tell him my Design to prove my Innocence—and when his Father comes, place both the Old Men in that Window there, where they may see all; Away, I hear him coming.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—have you consider'd then, Madam? Will you allow me a Man of Wit now? ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Nay, I confess I deserve you shou'd laugh at me for sending to ye—but I swear I was not able to let you go, till you had ask't my pardon for the affront you put upon me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
