prose: An affront? not in the least 'faith—a little harmless rallery, that was all—why thou art not such a Fool to think my Father believ'd me, Do'st? No, no, he knew I was in Jest.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Now is he going about another Swinger—well, I believe I have the lying'st Son of a Whore to my Master that ever was born-fifty an hour is nothing to him.—

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: A Jest?—what your swearing that I shut ye into the Press with Intent to have you lye with me? a Jest?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Nothing else upon my Faith.—Come, let all be forgot; and since we have given proof of one another's Wit—let us now

come to the tryal of our Persons—Come my Dear—your promise—Pox, must

This Creature molest us now?—Prithee send the Bawd of an errand.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Promise, or not Sir—you are like to stay till we are married, I'll assure ye—Well, are they come? and have you plac'd 'em as I order'd ye?

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Yes, Madam, there in that Window—look up, you may see 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ha, ha, ha,—the Rogue has her there.—Now I shall see if he behaves himself like a Cock of Four, or no.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: And I shall see how she behaves her self—but Mum—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come, prithee leave whispering; These Young Bawds are never good for any thing but mischief.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: She shall be gone immediately—but first for the safety of my Honour, confess before her—that what you sed in the Hall before my Father, was a lye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Well, I confess it was—now begone Mistris, be gone I say; and do you, Sirrah, hide your self below till I come, and be sure you are not seen.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Hold, I must have a word with him first—be gone, and get the Rope ready.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: With Him?—Pox, prithee lose none of thy breath with Him, let Him go.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: 'Tis for your safety, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: So, now the Old Woman's gone—now Cock of Four.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Friend, there is a weighty business impos'd upon you, for your Master's good; for Sir Ferdinand had never pull'd him by the Ears—if Pomgranats had been in season. Now you being a Schollar, and Homer you know loving Paremains—sent all the Lobsters in the Levant to Massinello the Fisher-man—You understand me?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Yes, yes—gads noons not a word—not I—You say, Madam, that I being a Scholar, proceed—pray.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
You, I say, having read Aristotle—and knowing Mice to be very destructive to the Common-Wealth, cannot but consider what your Master may suffer; for there is as much difference in Perrukes, as in Bucklers, and the Cardinal Bobinello loosing one of his Teeth with a Skirmish 'twixt him, and the Pigmies—Your Master's

Interest will be left in the hand of Sir Ieoffry, or the Heere Hander van Dander Scopen; D'ee conceive me?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Yes, yes, I think I do. Madam, I speak 8. Languages; I assure ye therefore, I think I understand ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come, come, Madam—what business can she have with this dull Rogue?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Oh she is ready I see—Now Sir, I come to ye.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
prose:
Nay Sir, no struggling,

our Power shall master ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Damn'd, Cowardly Dogs—and damn'd dull Rogue as I was to venture my self here, knowing her so well.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: What, you are running away, Sirrah, are ye? come, the Rope, the Rope quickly.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: O mercy, mercy! Why you will not be guilty of such barbarity, will you? to hang up 8 Languages?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: How, how, Tom? beset, and bound—then 'tis time to discover my self—Courage, Tom—Courage, I am here—I'm here.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Ay, and I am here too, Sir—nay, sit still—for here's no getting out.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose:
How Sir Peregreene—'S'bud, this was a Plot,

I find it now.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: So, this Service has oblig'd me—but now begone all, and leave him to me.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: My Father here too! Pox, this is worst of all—Oh I cou'd curse now! well, he that loves a Woman, loves his Torment—and he that Courts her—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, have you consider'd yet, Sir?—will ye allow me a Woman of Wit now? Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—a Rare Girle I profess.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ha, ha, ha; well, I was a damn'd Insipid Rogue, that's the truth on't—but Madam, little did I think you cou'd have been thus ungrateful.

speeches.speaker: Cell.
prose: Ungrateful! why thou shallow inconsiderate unthinking fool, Cou'dst thou Imagine I cou'd sleep—and leave thy last affront unpunish't? No, all my Faculties were turn'd to Thought & Revenge. Nor get ye your Liberty, till I have it throughly.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: But what harm did I do, Madam? You know I took your part—oh—

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: What, Sirrah, are you prating? I'll stop your noise.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Well, I shall get loose agen—and then if you persist in this usage, I shall then be implacable—You know, Madam, I have Wit.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: What, d'ee threaten me?—I know you have Wit; Where, where is it? for my part, I am blind to it; but I can give ye some, Sir—thus—and thus—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Who' Pox—Prithee forbear—'S'death, this is barbarous.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: O, 'tis a blessing you want, Sir—and pray let me infuse it into ye—You cheated me, I remember, with your broken Legg, last Night Sir, and roar'd, and howl'd, and laugh't and fool'd me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Oh Devil, this is past sufferance.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Told a swinging lye this morning to prove me a Whore, Sir, to my Father; for which there is a swinging cuff, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Umph—nay enough, enough—come—I'll reform.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: And so will I too—I'll never Pimp for him, no—oh—

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Still prating, Rascal?

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Oh that plaguy Quean—that brought me hither.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: You must have patience, Sir—a sweet Girle I profess.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: What, is the Monsieur catch't?—the plotting Monsieur? Ha, ha, ha—this is strange I swear Sir—where was all your Wit?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Dam her, Is she come too?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose:
Ay, where indeed—ah Cousin, he's so cruel to me, here have I lain languishing this hour,

and not so much as a kind word from him.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ah Devil!

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Ha, ha, ha—what, and his Spaniel here too? What, Sirrah, Cannot your 8 Languages free ye from that Rope?

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ah, wou'd they cou'd.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Now I think on't—I shou'd bestow a little Wit on you, Sirrah—my Lying—Pimping—Ugly Impudent Varlet—There's for ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Oh! wou'd my Master had been hang'd seven years ago, rather than I had come to this—oh—

speeches.speaker: Lucill.
prose: Again Rogue, agen; ah 'tis gone.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Oones I am deliver'd by Miracle; Look up, Sir, look up—I am free—Nay, 'faith Madam, I beg your pardon, I must be Porter now.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: How? free? nay then, Fate is mine agen, Sirrah, lock the Door, and take out the Key.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: 'Tis done, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Come then, unbind me quickly.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Cur'st Accident—Catch't agen?—help, help.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Help, help.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ay, Faith—I'll help ye presently, Your humble Servant, and Devoted Lover, Madam, is making what haste he can.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: How! at Liberty?—Nay then 'tis time to help indeed.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: By Bacchus, Sir, but you shall not—now 'tis my turn to be Porter; Now Son Thomas—now Cock of Four—now Rogue, now.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose:
Sirrah, for this piece of Service—there's a Lady for ye;

Take her, be thankful, and multiply.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: Ha, ha—with all my heart 'faith—come Madam, 'gad I have not had a touch a great while.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Ha, ha, ha,—ha, ha, ha, what think ye now, Madam? Wheres your Wit now?—Did I not tell you what a stubborn denyal must come to? 'gad if thou scap'st me now—let me be recorded an Ass, and my Story put into a Ballad.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Nay, do not dishonour me good Sir; if you love me—I'm sure you will not—I confess I have wrong'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Dam Confessions, Madam—do that when the business is done, and then I'll confess with ye.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: And I must confess too.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Kind, Dear Sweet Sir, help, help!

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Well sed Tom, Well sed Tom, to her agen Son Thomas, to her agen Boy—ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Rascal, Villain, Debauch'd Villain, thou wilt not ravish her, wilt thou?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: No, no, Sir, upon my Faith not I; I.ll onely lye with her, that's all.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: Why, thou wilt not lye with her before my face?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Yes but I will tho'—and before my own Father's face too; But for your sake, Sir, I ll use her as kindly as I can.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: 'Gads noones, this is sport.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Savage, Barb'rous Villain—oh Heaven! what sin have I committed, to undergo this punishment? help, help; help—

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Rather kill me Sir, than do it. Help, help.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Apox on 'em—they have taken the Alarm—I see—'gad I must dispatch—I find I shall be hinder'd else.

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Help, help,—I'm undone else—help, help.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'S'death! What Barbarity is this?—what were you going to do with the Lady, Sir? ha?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Why, I was going to teach her a new Dance, Val.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Ay, I believe 'twas a Dance indeed.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per,
prose: Kill him, kill him—let him be murder'd—let me come to him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hold, hold Sir—this must not be in my house.

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: I ll lay the Statute of Ravishment against him, I'll have him hang'd, I'll take the Law on him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: You take a Coxcomb, will you?—Tom, give me thy hand, Fifteen hundred a year is thy own for this dayes work; And now talk of the Law, Sir, if you dare—Tom and I will swinge ye.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: Now, Madam, cou'd not you have sav'd all this, and been willing?

speeches.speaker: Cellid.
prose: Impudent Man! cou'd no entreaty prevail with ye? Well, from this instant I'll shun thee as I wou'd the Plague; and if I do speak of thee, it shall be with Scorn, and Derision—to curse thy ill Nature—and Ingratitude—to which purpose I this Moment banish all sparks of Love—and do here solemnly vow—Never to see thee more.

speeches.speaker: Sabin.
prose: Nor I, unless it be to revenge this baseness.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: A Pox on't, this comes of Interruption, if they had but stay'd a little longer, that I might have had earnest of her, all had been sure;—but one Weeks humble Address shall make all well agen, shall it not, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Per.
prose: No Sir, Not believe I'll put up this affront so tamely: You shall hear from me, assure your self.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Ah, let him go, Tom—the Old Fool frets—ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Launce.
prose: A Pox on't, I have had the greatest Loss—for methought my Nymph began to be willing.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Thou wilt?

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I warrant ye, Sir, And now to you my Friends—first Val. I beg thy pardon for offering this in thy house—Prithee forget all—and from this Minute—assure thy self—I am thy Friend indeed.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well Sir—having some Interest in the rest of your Frollicks, I have the more reason to bear with this—especially since 'twas onely a Design—But had you gone through with your Dance—You and I shou'd have made but a kind of a scurvy Salutation.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: For thy sake onely, I am glad it hapned otherwise—Dear Franck, give me thy hand too.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
prose: With all my heart—and believe I share a great deal of content in seeing you two friends; for when I came in first—I guest it wou'd be otherwise—

speeches.speaker: Tho.
prose: I believe thou did'st.—What Iack art thou behind? here come forth, and give me thy hand too—Come, all is forgot; Thou art a damn'd Inconstant Rogue, I believe thou wilt confess it: but let that pass. We have all our failings.

speeches.speaker: Hyl.
prose: We have so—but this Kindness in thee has so oblig'd me—that I am resolv'd to desert my Roaring Humour, and turn all into Friendship for thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Wild.
prose: Well sed Cock of Four—'gad I like it well—Come Gentlemen—Pray let me Invite ye to my house—I'll provide a Collation, and we'l be heartily merry.

speeches.speaker: Tho.
verse: Loose Love like a thin Garment serves us ill,
And though wee'r pleas'd with it, we shiver still;
But I'm confirm'd, let th' Age be what it will,
What ever Nature in a Miss design'd,
Wives only are the Blessing of Mankind.
prose: Come, you shall go 'faith—for I am resolv'd to give my farewel to Intrigues, with a free and merry heart; and 'tis fit that you that are my Friends, shou'd be now my Witnesses, as you shall be when I go through the t'other Gate, Marriage. And tho' this kind of life is least troublesome; t'other is certainly most safe: especially, if a Man can change his Temper, else 'tis a Plague to him. For Marriage to a Debauchee, is a second Purgatory; It gives him onely a Prospect of Joy, or Torment, without knowing which he shall arrive to. But I hope I know my self better, than to venture without great Consideration to such Uncertainties.
